introduction: “It is forbidden you to trade in slaves, be they men or women.” The Kitáb-i-Aqdas, in 1873, prohibits slavery outright, on the ground that all are servants of one Lord and none may own another. The guide’s four passages are that law, a prayer of Bahá’u’lláh written on freeing a slave, and two reminiscences of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá. Job saw the principle, “did not he that made me in the womb make him?”; Leviticus proclaimed liberty at the jubilee; Paul called a runaway slave “a brother beloved” and sent him back; the Qur’an counted freeing a slave among the highest acts. None forbade the institution.
questions: On what ground does the reading forbid slavery? Why is that ground stronger than kindness?
Paul called Onesimus a brother and returned him to his owner. What does that show about the distance between a principle and a law?
What present arrangements might a later age see as we see slavery?

outside.why: It is not for him who is himself a servant to buy another of God’s servants. Job, of his own bondservants: did not he that made me in the womb make him?
The jubilee law, later cast on the Liberty Bell: proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof.
One slave standing at the door of another, seeking his freedom. Paul sending Onesimus back to his master: not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved.

The story of Isfandíyár, who stayed and served when he might have gone. The Qur’an names the steep ascent of virtue: it is to free a slave. Paul sent a slave back; the Qur’an commends freeing one; Bahá’u’lláh forbade the trade outright. Why did the earlier scriptures stop short of prohibition?
